_meta.purpose: SRC-4 (AuditLab, 2026-08-14): mechanically-derived inventory of every record carrying a sourcing gap/verification note, regenerated on every preship_gate.py run so it can never go stale or be a remembered subset.

entries.note: Corrected during sprint-task-5 adversarial verify: initial spike data used 'before July 1' loosely and computed a July 1 deadline; re-checked directly against the NC Board's own 2025-2026 renewal page, which states the cutoff is June 30 (July 1 is when the Letter-of-Demand process starts). Fixed to June 30 with the primary source URL updated accordingly. Downgraded to a data gap during the 2026-07-05 correctness audit after the source page went briefly dead. RE-OPENED 2026-07-06 (P2 gap-closure pass): re-confirmed 21 NCAC 08J .0101's current text and initially treated 'by the first day of July' and the Board's 'June 30' as the same instant described two ways -- WRONG. CORRECTED 2026-07-06 per the orchestrator's independent adversarial verification: these are two different calendar dates (July 1 vs. June 30), and the codified rule is the legally controlling text, not the Board's operational webpage. Publishing 2027-07-01 (the codified date), not 2027-06-30.

Michigan's renewal rule is confirmed by two official sources: LARA's licensing page and Mich. Admin. Code R 339.1003(1), both stating that an individual CPA license expires biennially on July 31. Neither source states which year of the two-year cycle applies to a given license, so no single "next July 31" date applies to every CPA. Check your license or the Michigan Board of Accountancy (LARA) for your specific renewal year.

Texas's own licensing rule (22 TAC 515.3) confirms this directly: individual CPA licenses have staggered expiration dates tied to your own birth month, so your renewal is due by the last day of that month each year. The board's own renewal page tells CPAs the same thing, so the codified rule and the board agree on this cycle. The annual renewal fee itself isn't fixed in the rule -- the board sets that amount each year, on top of a separate $10.00 Scholarship Trust Fund fee that is fixed by rule. Because the fee is set by board action rather than written into the rule, it can change from year to year without a rule filing -- confirm the current figure with the board when you renew.

Your New Jersey CPA license renews on a personal, rolling triennial (3-year) cycle -- three years from your own license's last expiration date, not a shared calendar date for every licensee. N.J.A.C. 13:29-1.7(b) sets this out directly, and the same three-year clock applies to your first renewal too. Confirm your exact date on your license certificate or with the Board.

New Jersey firm registration renews on the same personal, rolling triennial cycle as individual licenses -- three years from your firm's own last registration date, not one shared calendar date for every firm. Confirm your firm's exact renewal date with the New Jersey State Board of Accountancy or on your registration certificate.

Massachusetts CPA licenses renew every 2 years, always on June 30, on a fixed odd- or even-year parity that's permanent once assigned -- a lapsed license returns to its original parity, never a new one. Which parity a brand-new license starts on isn't stated in the statute, in 252 CMR, or on any Board page -- we checked all of them. The Board's FAQ CPE table and the Mass. Society of CPAs point to a 'second June 30 after issuance' rule, but neither is Board-published, so we still don't compute a date from it. Confirm your renewal year with the Board (617-701-8635) or via eLIPSE.

Massachusetts CPA licenses renew every 2 years, always on June 30, on a fixed odd- or even-year parity that's permanent once assigned -- a lapsed license returns to its original parity, never a new one. Which parity a brand-new license starts on isn't stated in the statute, in 252 CMR, or on any Board page -- we checked all of them. The Board's FAQ CPE table and the Mass. Society of CPAs point to a 'second June 30 after issuance' rule, but neither is Board-published, so we still don't compute a date from it. Confirm your renewal year with the Board (617-701-8635) or via eLIPSE.

Your Maryland renewal date is personal to your license, not shared across all CPAs. The Board describes a personal month/day anniversary (e.g. issued January 2, expires January 2), and a check of real, active license records confirms that pattern is genuinely in use today -- including licenses outside December and in odd years. Maryland's statute also sets a Dec-31/even-year fallback, and at least one active license shows exactly that date, so not every license follows the anniversary rule. Look up your own date via NASBA's CPAverify (ald.nasba.org/search/cpa).

Tennessee assigns each individual CPA certificate and PA registration to one of two biennial renewal cohorts by license number (odd or even), so no single date applies to everyone -- this is now codified at Tenn. Code Ann. Sec 62-1-107(b), not just Board guidance. Firm permits are a separate, still-open question: the codified rule sets them to expire annually, but the Board's current guidance runs firms on the same biennial cycle as individuals, with no rule change pending. Confirm your exact date and cohort with the Board.

2026-07-16 follow-up (per orchestrator instruction not to spin further, just keep this honest): tried one more avenue -- the aggregate Iowa Administrative Bulletin for 6/10/2026 (legis.iowa.gov/docs/aco/bulletin/06-10-2026.pdf) does exist and is reachable (corrects the prior note's 'not in the regular IAB bulletin index' -- it is indexed, at that exact date), but the PDF itself is image-based/encrypted (pdftotext: "Unknown filter 'Crypt'"; WebFetch independently confirmed the same -- "a heavily compressed JPEG image embedded within a PDF structure") and not text-extractable by either method, so ARC 1582Z's entry within it could not be read. Combined with the filing detail page (rules.iowa.gov/Notice/Details/1582Z) itself having no subject/summary/effective-date populated, this remains a genuinely unresolved lead, not a dead one -- three independent access methods now tried. June 30 is very likely still correct (rule text independently confirmed current against ARC 7681C, eff. 4/10/24, which verbatim-supports June 30) but this record should not be treated as fully current until 1582Z's content is confirmed by a human opening the filing directly or contacting Iowa LSA/the Board. 2026-07-13 audit (original): first surfaced this gap. || 2026-08-14 renumbering fix: All Iowa Admin. Code 193A accountancy chapters were editorially transferred to Inspections and Appeals [481] chapters 1021-1040 by IAC Supplement 2026-06-10 (2023 Iowa Acts SF 514); the old 193A chapter PDFs are now transfer-notice stubs. Old citation 193A-5.3(1) is now 481-1025.3(1) -- the full Chapter 1025 PDF was fetched and the operative sentence ('Licenses expire on June 30 of each year', 1025.3(1)) plus the 30-day grace/lapse rule (1025.4(2)) confirmed verbatim, chapter header itself records 'Prior to 6/10/26, see Accountancy Examining Board[193A] Ch 5'.

December 31 of every even-numbered year is the DC Board of Accountancy's renewal date for both the individual CPA license and the firm permit. Only the firm permit's date is codified: 17 DCMR § 2547.1 sets it for permits issued under § 2542, a firm-specific term distinct from an individual license. The DCMR's accountancy chapter (17-25) contains no section setting the individual license's own term, and the DC Code's general renewal statute (§ 47-2853.13) delegates term length to law or regulation without stating it. A separate Title 17 chapter does set a generic license-term rule for several other DC occupational boards (17 DCMR § 3306), but its own scope section names those boards specifically and doesn't include the Board of Accountancy, so it doesn't reach the individual CPA license either. The individual license's date comes from the Board's published guidance rather than a codified rule.

2026-08-21 (AuditLab CITE-42, self-directed fix): re-fetched cpa4060.pdf directly and read past the sentence this record already cited. The form states the biennial period applies 'regardless of the date of issuance, except licenses issued within 90 days of the expiration date which are issued to the next biennial expiration date' -- an undisclosed cohort exception the record's cycle_description didn't model. A CPA first licensed Oct-Dec 2027 is actually due 2029-12-31, not 2027-12-31; the site would have told them to renew ~8 weeks after being licensed. Added a plain sentence to cycle_description rather than a cohort_groups entry (the window is narrow and time-bounded, so prose is proportionate per AuditLab's own recommendation). next_deadline_computed unchanged -- it is still correct for the general population; the exception is disclosed, not computed per-visitor, matching how this site already handles Idaho's operational-guidance lag.

2026-07-16 follow-up (see also 2026-07-13 note below): independently re-confirmed both AS 08.04.105(a) and 12 AAC 04.189 (License Renewal) directly via the Board's own hosted CPARegulations.pdf (pdftotext-extracted) -- neither states the specific December 31 date or the odd-year pattern for individual licenses. The statute text is not retrievable at any reachable host: akleg.gov's statutes page (re-confirmed 2026-08-20) returns 200 with a live navigation-stub page ('This page is no longer used please use www.akleg.gov') containing zero occurrences of the statute -- a moved page serving nothing at the destination, not a refused request. The parallel firm-permit rule (12 AAC 04.280(c)) DOES explicitly state a renewal is 'due not later than December 31' -- strong indirect corroboration that individuals share the same calendar -- but that is not a direct citation for the individual-license date specifically, so the citation/Verified badge was removed from this record rather than left pointing at a rule that doesn't itself establish the displayed date. The date is very likely correct (math, Board materials, and the firm-rule corroboration all agree) but is not verbatim-confirmed against an individual-specific codified provision. 2026-07-13 amendment-currency audit (original): unverified, akleg.gov's statute pages serve no rule text; candidates for the individual-specific cite (12 AAC 04.189, 12 AAC 02.935) remain unconfirmed; a related 2025 regulation package (12 AAC 04, eff. 7/26/2025) also unconfirmed as to scope. Pending a human browser check of akleg.gov/basis/aac.asp directly, or of 12 AAC 02.935 specifically.

2026-07-16 follow-up: independently confirmed 12 AAC 04.280(c) directly via the Board's own hosted regulations PDF (pdftotext-extracted, not a summarized fetch) -- it explicitly states a firm-permit renewal application is 'due not later than December 31' for the biennial license period. This resolves the earlier uncertainty about whether the cited rule actually establishes the displayed date: for firms, it does. The specific odd-year pattern (that the current period ends in 2027, not 2026) is not itself spelled out in this section, but is corroborated by the Board's own published materials and the arithmetic of a continuous biennial cycle. The statute text is not retrievable at any reachable host: akleg.gov's statutes page (re-confirmed 2026-08-20) returns 200 with a live navigation-stub page ('This page is no longer used please use www.akleg.gov') containing zero occurrences of the statute -- a moved page serving nothing at the destination, not a refused request; this confirmation relies on the Board's own hosted copy of the regulation text instead. 2026-07-13 amendment-currency audit (original, superseded by the above): flagged this record as unverified pending exactly this check.

2026-08-20 (CITE-13 labelling fix, AuditLab): cycle_description was attributing the specific 2026-2027 window to 12 AAC 04.280 itself, but the rule only establishes the biennial mechanic and the Dec 31 deadline, never naming which window is current -- exactly the gap this note already documented above. Reworded to separate what the rule states from what the Board's materials + arithmetic confirm; no change to the date itself, which was already right.

Your Vermont firm registration renews every two years -- confirmed by both the statute (26 V.S.A. § 75(a)) and Board Rule 6.1(d). The specific July 31/odd-year date, though, is written into the codified rule (Rule 8.1(b)) for "Licenses" only; that text is never extended to firm registrations. Vermont's Office of Professional Regulation applies the same July 31/odd-year date to firms in practice, listing it for every Accountancy license and firm type on its own official fee and renewal-date table. So the two-year cycle is codified law, and the July 31 date for firms comes from the regulator's own published table rather than from the statute or rule text itself.

Rhode Island assigns each permit to one of three rotating three-year cohorts through board discretion, not a public formula -- the three cohorts trace to a one-time 2008 transitional provision that let the board assign 1-, 2-, or 3-year transitional permits at its discretion, and every permit since simply keeps the expiration year it was first given. No public input (license number, birth month, year first licensed, etc.) determines your cohort. Check your permit or contact the Rhode Island Board of Accountancy to confirm which year yours expires.

You can rely on DC's 80-hour biennial requirement (with a 4-hour ethics minimum) -- it's confirmed in two independent places that agree: 17 DCMR §§2530.1 and 2530.8, and the Board's own CPE Reporting Form, which quotes both sections verbatim. DC's online regulations portal doesn't offer a stable link to individual sections -- its section-list page resolves to a search screen, not the rule text -- so the citation above points you directly to the Board's reporting form PDF, the official document that reproduces the rule's language.

Georgia has two official versions of this rule in circulation and they don't agree. The Secretary of State's site (rules.sos.ga.gov/gac/20-11) still shows the superseded pre-2024 text -- 80 hours with 16 in accounting and auditing, and no ethics requirement. The current rule is the Board's own Rule 20-11-.02, amended effective January 1, 2024, which sets today's 50%-technical-fields and ethics requirements; that is what this record follows and what actually governs your CPE. If the Secretary of State's site shows different numbers, that's why.

Nebraska's 80-hour CPE figure is confirmed by two sources: the statute (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 1-136.01) sets the requirement in days, converted using the standard 8-hours-per-day basis every CPE-day-based state statute uses, and the Nebraska Board of Public Accountancy's current published guidance states the resulting 80 hours directly. The 4-hour ethics requirement is directly codified at 288 Neb. Admin. Code ch. 8, § 004.01.

The 120-hour/3-year total is confirmed in both SDCL 36-20B-27's statutory text ("120 hours of continuing education in each three-year renewal period") and the board's own FAQ. The 20-hour annual minimum appears only on the board's FAQ -- we haven't found it in the statute or in the administrative rule chapter (whose only annual-minimum language covers the initial-certificate phase-in period, not general renewal). It comes from the board itself, so plan to report at least 20 hours each year; the gap here is that we can't point to codified text for it, not that it's optional.

Heads-up: Act 2026-16 (the "Pathways to CPA Act") amends Code of Ala. 1975 §34-1-11 effective October 1, 2026. The reinstatement fee cap, the per-lapsed-year back-fees and CPE catch-up, and the September 30 expiration / December 31 renewal-filing dates on this page carry over unchanged -- the amendment's changes to this subsection are stylistic renumbering, not substance. If you're reinstating on or after October 1, 2026, confirm you're citing the current section numbering with the Board.

D.C. doesn't set this fee by codified rule: no DCMR fee schedule states the $295. The Board sets its fees administratively under D.C. Code §47-2853.10 and publishes the current amounts on its own page -- the same way DC handles its other licensing fees. Because the amount isn't fixed by rule, it can change without a rule filing, so confirm the current figure with the Board before you pay. The 40-hour-per-year CPE reinstatement requirement (capped at 120 hours) is codified in 17 DCMR §2530.3; the citation link above points to D.C. Code §47-2851.10 instead because the District publishes stable per-section web addresses only for the D.C. Code, not for individual DCMR sections.

Confirmed directly from the codified fee rule, not just the Board's own page: HAR §16-53-38 sets the restoration formula as the biennial renewal fee plus an equal penalty fee (paragraphs (7) and (11)), and HRS §26-9(o) separately requires any unpaid fee -- including the $100 biennial Compliance Resolution Fund fee under HAR §16-53-38(12) -- to be paid to restore a license. For an individual license: $52 renewal + $52 penalty + $100 Compliance Resolution Fund fee = $204. For a non-sole-proprietorship firm permit: $130 + $130 + $100 = $360. Sole-proprietorship firm permits owe no Compliance Resolution Fund fee under (12), so their total stops at $64 + $64 = $128. These published figures are the baseline for restoring within the same biennium; HAR §16-53-38(8) and HRS §466-8(c) add a further $20 recordkeeping fee for each full biennium your license was on forfeited status.

Louisiana's reinstatement fee isn't a single number under Louisiana law: which of three mechanisms applies depends on how long your certificate has been lapsed. A same-year reinstatement uses the renewal fee plus a board-prescribed penalty fee, with no fixed dollar amount codified (LAC 46:XIX Sec1105.B.6). A fully expired or inactive certificate instead goes through a formal reinstatement application, capped by statute at $500 (La. R.S. 37:74.1). Separately, the board's own fee table applies an escalating monthly delinquent fee of $200-$700 depending on how many months have passed. These mechanisms don't reconcile with one another, which is why they don't reduce to one figure. The 3-hour ethics-CPE figure comes from the board's own page; the codified rule text (Sec1301, Sec1303, Sec1319) does not itself state an hour figure.

The $57 late fee and $161 renewal fee come from the Board of Public Accountancy's own current fee pages, not from 252 CMR 2.16 itself -- read the rule's full text and you won't find a dollar figure anywhere in it. It describes reinstatement fees only as "the back license fee," "a late fee," and "the current license fee" (or "current license renewal fee"), leaving the actual amounts for the board to set administratively rather than fixing them in the rule text, so they can change without a formal rule amendment. The CPE side works differently: it's codified directly in statute, where M.G.L. c. 112, Sec 87B(c) sets the 160-hour/24-month requirement for a license lapsed two or more renewal cycles, including the rule that at least 80 of those hours must be in the attest function.

Michigan's statutes and rules don't state this $320 total in any single line -- you assemble it from three components: the $100 application-processing fee, the $20 late-renewal fee, and $200 for the upcoming two-year license period. The board's own licensing guide confirms the assembled figure ("2 year CPA Relicensure Application and Fee: $320.00"), independently matching what the law requires.

The $20 fee is set directly in Minnesota statute, so that's the source you'll see cited here. The board's own site covers the reinstatement process but doesn't state the dollar amount -- which is why the statute, not a board page, is the authority behind this figure.

Nevada doesn't have one flat reinstatement fee or CPE figure -- which one applies depends on your situation, because the state codifies three separate tracks. A simple late renewal (paid before the lapse goes further) costs a $150 late fee on top of the standard $175 annual fee. Reinstatement from retired or inactive status costs $250 and requires 40 CPE hours, including 4 in ethics, completed in the preceding 12 months. Reinstatement after voluntary surrender requires 40 hours plus payment of back fees. Reinstatement after revocation or disciplinary surrender requires 80 hours, including 8 in ethics, in the preceding 12 months. A missed renewal doesn't convert to revocation automatically: failing to obtain the annual permit within 60 days of expiration is a ground for the board to revoke, unless excused -- it is a board decision, not an automatic outcome. These are three distinct, separately codified paths (NAC 628.016, NAC 628.110), not one number with exceptions, so no single reinstatement fee or CPE-hours figure would accurately represent every case -- check which track applies to you before paying or scheduling CPE.

Ohio doesn't publish one flat reinstatement fee because state law itself sets a formula, not a flat number, as laid out above. That's confirmed on two independent fronts: the Ohio Revised Code spells out the per-month rates and caps, and the Accountancy Board's own fees page (under its 'Late and Back Fees' tab) states the identical figures -- $50/month (capped at $300) for a registration or permit, $100/month (capped at $1,200) for a permit holder employed in public accounting.

The $225 reinstatement fee, $255 biennial renewal fee, and 16-hour CPE penalty are all set out in Oregon's codified rules (OAR 801-010-0010 and 801-010-0130) -- the same rule text cited above. The Board's renewal-information page describes the lapse and reinstatement process in plain terms but doesn't restate these specific figures; the rule itself is the definitive source for them.

You can rely on the $500 reinstatement fee, $375 renewal fee, and 120-hour CPE requirement as stated directly in Rhode Island's codified accountancy rule -- not an estimate. The board's own renewal page independently confirms the lockout mechanic and cycle deadline that trigger reinstatement in the first place.

Both cited rules confirmed verbatim, word for word: ARSD 20:75:03:03 states "the fee for renewal is one hundred dollars" and "the annual late renewal fee is an additional one hundred dollars" for each year the certificate was expired -- that's the $100-plus-$100-per-lapsed-year formula above, not a single flat figure by design. ARSD 20:75:04:08 confirms the CPE side exactly: a certificate lapsed more than 12 months requires 24 hours of CPE in the preceding 12 months; lapsed 12 months or less requires only the normal CPE the applicant would have owed anyway.

Utah sets reinstatement fees administratively rather than codifying them in rule -- R156-26a contains no dollar figures anywhere in its text. The $113 total (and the $85 alternate for licenses expired more than two years with no unlicensed practice) comes directly from DOPL's own reinstatement application document, which is the fee's actual source of truth under this system. Because DOPL can revise that application without a rule filing, confirm the figure on the current application before paying.

Colorado doesn't put a dollar figure on this fee anywhere in law. Colo. Rev. Stat. 12-100-106 authorizes the CPA renewal fee, and 12-20-105 has DORA's Division of Professions and Occupations set the actual amount administratively, so it lives on DORA's own fee schedule instead of the statute book -- and it can change without a rule filing. That holds at the regulation level too: the State Board of Accountancy's own rules (3 CCR 705-1) spell out the renewal requirement and a 60-day grace period (you can still renew during it, but a late fee is added) without putting a number on either fee. DORA's online renewal portal won't show you a fee until you log in, and the FAQ and licensing-services pages that would normally carry it are currently returning "Access denied" to any visitor. Since the amount isn't published anywhere we can point you to, log in to DORA's online licensing portal or contact the Board directly to confirm your current fee before you renew.

D.C. doesn't codify this fee in a rule: neither DCMR Title 17 Chapter 25 (Board of Accountancy) nor Chapter 40 (general licensing) contains a fee schedule. The fee is set administratively instead, and the regulator publishes the current amounts on DLCP's Board of Accountancy page -- $110 for renewal, $50 for late renewal. Because the amount isn't fixed by rule, it can change without a rule filing, so confirm the current figure with DLCP before you pay.

Delaware doesn't publish a flat renewal fee, by design. State law (29 Del. C. 8735(c)) has the Division of Professional Regulation set license fees to cover its own costs rather than fixing a dollar figure in the code, and DPR's own fee page confirms it: you're notified of the amount directly when you renew. Since no schedule exists to publish, your renewal notice from DPR is the source for the current figure.

Maryland's $63 individual and $151 firm renewal fees are codified in COMAR 09.24.01.09B, and the Board's own fee page shows the same figures -- confirmed in both places. That regulation only sets the dollar amounts; your renewal cycle is biennial, and how your exact expiration date is determined is covered on this site's Maryland individual-license renewal page.

The $175 figure isn't codified -- NAC 628.016(3)(g) only caps whatever the Board sets at "will not exceed $200" a year, and NRS 628.380 delegates the actual amount to the Board. It's confirmed instead on the Nevada State Board of Accountancy's own official renewal page (nvaccountancy.com, which redirects to the Board's licensing portal): "the renewal fee will be $175" whether you submit online or by mail, with a $150 late fee if you miss the January 31 deadline. Because the amount is board-set rather than fixed in the statute or rule, it can change year to year without a rule filing -- confirm the current figure with the Board before you renew.

New Hampshire's statute delegates the exact fee amount to OPLC's own rulemaking rather than spelling it out itself. OPLC's fee rule (Plc 1002.01, Table 1002.1) sets it at $201 -- the same figure posted on OPLC's fee page, so it's confirmed in two independent sources.

The $135 triennial registration fee comes straight from New Jersey's codified rule, N.J.A.C. 13:29-1.5(a)3, which states it verbatim: "3. Triennial registration: $ 135.00." That rule was readopted without any changes in 2024, so this is a confirmed, current figure -- not a stale snapshot from the original 2018 adoption.

CNMI's codified administrative code still shows a $100 renewal fee -- that text hasn't changed. But CNMI's enabling statute, 4 CMC § 3422(b), makes clear a CPA certificate is issued and renewed on a three-year cycle, not annually, so the code table's "Renewal/annual" label is a legacy category name rather than a literal yearly requirement. CNMI's Board of Accountancy has no government website of its own -- NASBA administers CNMI licensing on the Board's behalf, and NASBA's current fee page lists the individual renewal fee at $355 for that same three-year (Sept 30-Dec 31) cycle. No CNMI government page states $355 directly, so this record keeps $100 as the codified figure, but the two sources disagree materially: verify the exact amount with NASBA or the Board before you pay.

Puerto Rico's CPA renewal fee isn't fixed in the law itself. 20 L.P.R.A. § 779 states three times that the license and renewal fee is set "según disponga la Junta y el Departamento de Estado" -- by the Board and Department of State, not the statute -- and no dollar figure appears anywhere in that section. The $50 renewal fee sometimes attributed to the 1945 law appears nowhere in its current text or in Ley Núm. 147 de 28 de agosto de 2014, which rewrote the section wholesale into today's wording -- and the arrangement is older than the wording: a 2011 NASBA renewal-instructions sheet already shows a $180 fee set under the same delegation. Puerto Rico's Dept. of State designates NASBA as the official administrator of CPA licensing and renewals, and that's where the actual dollar figures live: $225 for individual renewal, $275 if you file late, reconfirmed live on 2026-09-04. No Puerto Rico government page publishes that dollar figure itself -- it lives only on NASBA's site -- so this record's $225 traces to the government-designated administrator rather than to a Puerto Rico statute or regulation.

$112 has been the confirmed rate since TSBPA raised it from $97, effective September 1, 2024. A full year has now passed since the date any further increase would have taken effect (September 1, 2025), and a fresh check of TSBPA's news archive and a site search for "annual license fee" and "fee increase" -- the same channel the Board used to announce the 2017, 2019, and 2024 increases -- turns up no notice of any further increase, so $112 remains current. One thing about this fee is permanent, not a gap: 22 TAC 521.1 does not fix a dollar figure itself; it says the fee "shall be established by the board on an annual basis," so the number lives in the Board's own announcements, not the rule text, and any future change will appear there -- the rule will not restate it. Confirm the current amount with TSBPA before you pay.

Separately, on the citation: this points at the correct rule (22 TAC 521.1), confirmed by navigating the state's own rule browser and independently by a secondary mirror of the same rule text. Texas publishes the Administrative Code through a portal with no addressable per-rule web pages -- the link above is the portal's own summary page, reachable only through its real navigation tree, not a guessable direct link.

This fee is confirmed directly on the Virgin Islands Board's own official page: the $135 CPA permit renewal fee and the $25-per-month late fee (capped at $600) after the August 31 deadline both match what's posted there, most recently rechecked 2026-08-15. The U.S. Virgin Islands doesn't publish its Title 27 code text online, so no codified statute citation is available for this fee -- the board's own page is the authoritative source available.
